title: Parallel and Sequential Execution
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of parallel and sequential execution and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to parallel and sequential execution.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on parallel and sequential execution. Independent jobs can run in parallel; `needs` creates an explicit dependency when one job requires another job’s outputs or successful completion. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Independent jobs can run in parallel; `needs` creates an explicit dependency when one job requires another job’s outputs or successful completion. Use `needs` for dependencies, matrices for controlled combinations, conditions for deliberate branching, and concurrency/timeouts to prevent stale or unbounded work. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Parallel jobs
items.text: List the supported combinations explicitly and use `include`/`exclude` or `max-parallel` to control expansion. Keep all required configurations covered and avoid unnecessary duplicate jobs.

items.title: Sequential jobs
items.text: Declare job dependencies with `needs` and read prerequisite results or outputs through `needs.<job>`. Separate jobs do not share a runner workspace automatically.

items.title: Independent job execution
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.text: For identifying bottlenecks in a pipeline, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Designing safe parallel workflows
items.text: List the supported combinations explicitly and use `include`/`exclude` or `max-parallel` to control expansion. Keep all required configurations covered and avoid unnecessary duplicate jobs.

content_blocks.code:
name: Parallel checks and dependent build
on: [push, pull_request]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Lint check placeholder"
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Test check placeholder"
  build:
    needs: [lint, test]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Build after both checks pass"
content_blocks.expected_output: The lint and test jobs are independent and may run concurrently; the build waits for both to succeed.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Review the job graph in a disposable branch, then replace the `echo` placeholders with real lint/test/build commands.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Keep the `needs` links if the build depends on both checks; otherwise revise them intentionally.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to parallel and sequential execution. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain parallel and sequential execution, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Express dependencies and parallel work as a clear job graph with bounded execution and failure behavior.

content.task: Apply parallel and sequential execution to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: Independent jobs can run in parallel; `needs` creates an explicit dependency when one job requires another job’s outputs or successful completion.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Independent jobs can run in parallel; `needs` creates an explicit dependency when one job requires another job’s outputs or successful completion. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
